title: Engineering wants two quarters to rebuild the foundation
summary: A credible rewrite proposal, a credible commercial objection, and no way to test either without committing.

brief.role: You are the PM for the core platform team.
brief.company: Verdance, a 400-person company selling supply-chain planning software.
brief.context: Your principal engineer has proposed replacing the scheduling engine — the component that computes plans — over two quarters with four engineers. The current engine is eight years old, written by people who have left, and is now the bottleneck for three roadmap items the commercial team cares about. The CRO has said publicly that two quarters with no customer-visible output is 'not survivable' in a year where the company has a growth target it is behind on. Your head of engineering supports the proposal but says the estimate is 'two quarters if nothing surprises us'. You have to bring a recommendation to the planning committee in a week.
brief.objective: Decide whether, when, and in what shape the scheduling engine work happens.
brief.constraints: The platform team is four engineers. Two quarters is half the year. The growth target is behind. No additional headcount this year.
brief.task: Recommend a course of action and be explicit about the risks you are taking on.

evidenceCards.title: The engineering proposal
evidenceCards.content:
From the principal engineer:
'The scheduling engine recomputes the full plan on every change. That was fine at 10k SKUs; our largest customers are at 400k and the recompute takes 6-11 minutes. Everything downstream inherits that.

The rewrite makes it incremental — recompute only what changed. Expected recompute for a typical edit: under 4 seconds.

Two quarters, four engineers. That is the full replacement including the migration path and running both engines in parallel to verify identical output on production data.

What I cannot do is a partial version. The full-recompute assumption is in the data model, not just the algorithm. I have looked at incremental patches twice and both times the answer was that we would be building the new engine badly, inside the old one.

Risk I want on the record: two quarters assumes we do not find a customer relying on undocumented behaviour of the old engine. I would put that at maybe 40% and it could add six weeks.'

evidenceCards.title: Commercial impact
evidenceCards.content:
The three blocked roadmap items and what the commercial team attributes to them:
- Scenario comparison (compare two plans side by side): named in 9 open opportunities, roughly $2.1m in pipeline. Blocked because running two plans doubles the recompute cost.
- Real-time collaboration on plans: named in 4 opportunities, roughly $700k. Blocked by the recompute lock.
- Automated replanning on supply disruption: named in 6 opportunities, roughly $1.4m, and it is the item the CRO mentions most. Blocked because the recompute cannot run often enough.

CRO's position: 'We are 11% behind plan. I need something to sell in Q3, not a story about Q1 next year.'

Support data: 'plan is slow' is the second most common ticket category from customers over 100k SKUs, at roughly 45 tickets a month. Two of the four largest accounts have raised it in their last QBR. One has a renewal in Q4.

evidenceCards.title: What else has been tried or proposed
evidenceCards.content:
Options the team has explored:

1. Hardware: moving the largest customers to bigger instances cut recompute by roughly 30% last year and cost $40k/month extra. Another 30% is available for about $90k/month, and the head of infrastructure says that is the end of that road.

2. Caching layer in front of the current engine: two engineers, six weeks. Would make repeat views of an unchanged plan instant. Does nothing for edits, which is where the pain is. It would unblock none of the three roadmap items.

3. Building scenario comparison on the old engine anyway: possible, but each comparison costs two full recomputes, so 12-22 minutes for large customers. The principal engineer's view: 'We could ship it. It would demo well and be unusable for the customers who asked for it.'

4. A narrower rewrite of only the recompute path, leaving the data model alone: the principal engineer estimates this at one quarter but says it delivers roughly a 3x improvement rather than 100x, and the data model work would still be needed later.

5. Do the full rewrite with two engineers instead of four while the other two ship roadmap items: four quarters instead of two, per the head of engineering.

evidenceCards.title: Organisational history and trust
evidenceCards.content:
Verdance attempted a platform rewrite three years ago. It was estimated at six months, ran for fourteen, and was abandoned with the work partially merged. The current engine still contains two half-migrated modules from that effort. Several people on the planning committee were there.

The principal engineer joined after that and has shipped two large projects on time since, including the reporting rewrite last year, which was estimated at one quarter and took one quarter plus two weeks.

The head of engineering's note: 'The difference from three years ago is that this one has a verification strategy — running both engines on production data and diffing the output. The last one had no way to know if it was working until it was finished.'

The planning committee includes the CRO, the CFO, the head of engineering, and your head of product. The CFO's stated concern is the extra $90k/month if hardware is used as a bridge.

decisionPrompt: What do you recommend to the planning committee?

decisionOptions.label: Full rewrite, four engineers, with parallel-run verification and a public checkpoint at week 8
decisionOptions.description: Commit the two quarters, use the dual-engine diff as the visible progress signal, and set an agreed checkpoint where the committee can stop or continue based on measured output-equivalence.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The committee approves after a hard session, mostly because the checkpoint gives them an exit the last rewrite never had.
At week 8 the parallel run shows 99.6% output equivalence on production data and a demonstrated 40x recompute improvement on a real customer dataset. The CRO's objection softens; he starts pre-selling automated replanning on a dated commitment rather than a hope.
The undocumented-behaviour risk materialises in month five — one customer depended on a rounding quirk — and adds five weeks. The engine ships in week 31 rather than 26. The three roadmap items ship over the following quarter.
Trade-off: you spent two and a half quarters and a hard committee fight to remove a bottleneck permanently, and the growth target for the year was missed on schedule rather than on capability.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale engages with the failed rewrite in the company's history, uses the parallel-run diff as an evidence-producing checkpoint rather than a promise, and states an explicit stop condition.

decisionOptions.label: Buy time with hardware, defer the rewrite to next year
decisionOptions.description: Spend the extra $90k/month on infrastructure for the largest customers, ship what can be shipped on the old engine, and revisit the rewrite when the growth target is met.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The 30% improvement lands within a month and 'plan is slow' tickets fall by about a third. The CFO is unhappy about $1.08m annualised for a temporary fix.
The three roadmap items remain blocked, so the $4.2m of named pipeline does not convert. Two opportunities are lost to a competitor citing scenario comparison specifically.
A year later the engine is the same engine, the largest customers are larger, and the rewrite proposal returns unchanged except that it is now three quarters.
Trade-off: you protected this year's shipping capacity and paid for it in cash, in pipeline, and in a problem that grew while you waited.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: The infrastructure head has said this road ends. Low credit unless the rationale argues something specific about why deferring is right despite the pipeline evidence and the growing dataset sizes.

decisionOptions.label: One-quarter narrow rewrite of the recompute path
decisionOptions.description: Take the 3x improvement in a single quarter, unblock what it unblocks, and decide about the data model afterwards.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The narrow rewrite lands in a quarter plus one week. Recompute for large customers goes from 6-11 minutes to about 2-4 minutes. 'Plan is slow' tickets fall by half.
Scenario comparison becomes buildable but slow — 4-8 minutes per comparison — and ships in the following quarter to mixed reception. Real-time collaboration and automated replanning remain blocked; both need the data model change.
The data model rewrite is proposed again nine months later, now with the narrow rewrite partially in the way. The principal engineer's estimate for it goes from two quarters to two and a half.
Trade-off: you bought visible progress in one quarter and made the eventual full rewrite somewhat harder while unblocking one of three items.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: A genuinely defensible compromise. Credit when the rationale acknowledges it addresses one of three blocked items and raises the later cost, rather than presenting it as the best of both worlds.

decisionOptions.label: Two engineers on the rewrite, two on roadmap, four quarters
decisionOptions.description: Keep customer-visible output flowing while the rewrite proceeds in the background at half speed.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Roadmap output continues at a reduced rate; the CRO gets two smaller features in Q3, neither of them the three that matter.
The rewrite runs for four quarters. In month seven a reorganisation moves one of the two rewrite engineers, and the timeline extends again. The parallel-run verification is built but rarely run because nobody has time to investigate diffs.
At month eleven the project is 70% complete and has consumed more total engineering time than the four-engineer version would have, and the committee members who remember the last rewrite start using the same language they used about it.
Trade-off: you avoided the hard conversation and produced the outcome the organisation most feared.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Low. Longer rewrites are more exposed to reorganisation and attrition, and this recreates the failure pattern in the company's own history. Only credit if the rationale confronts that history and argues against it specifically.

rubric.referenceReasoning: Both sides are right about their own domain: the engine genuinely blocks $4.2m of named pipeline and the CRO genuinely cannot survive two silent quarters. What resolves it is not compromise on scope but a change in what the committee gets to see. The last rewrite failed because nobody could tell whether it was working until it ended; this proposal has a parallel run producing measurable output-equivalence and a measurable speedup on real customer data from early on. That converts an unfalsifiable two-quarter promise into a series of checkpoints with a defined stop condition, which is the specific objection the organisation's history creates. A strong answer also prices the alternatives honestly: hardware is at the end of its road and costs $1.08m a year, the narrow rewrite unblocks one of three items and raises the later cost, and splitting the team makes a long project longer in an organisation that has already lost one long project to attrition. Finally, the 40% risk of a six-week overrun should be in the recommendation, not discovered later.
evidenceSignals: Uses the $4.2m of named pipeline across three blocked items rather than arguing debt in the abstract
Notices the infrastructure head has said the hardware path ends after the next 30%
Takes the failed rewrite three years ago seriously as an organisational constraint
Identifies the parallel-run diff as the mechanism that makes progress visible
Carries the principal engineer's own 40% overrun risk into the recommendation
Notes the narrow rewrite unblocks one of three items and raises the later cost

product_sense: Frames the engine as a constraint on what the company can sell, not as engineering housekeeping
Recognises shipping scenario comparison on the old engine would demo well and fail in use
analytics: Compares annualised hardware cost against the rewrite's engineering cost
Uses ticket volume and QBR escalations as evidence of customer impact
user_research: Uses the two largest accounts' QBR complaints and the Q4 renewal as concrete stakes
prioritization: Chooses between options on expected value rather than on who argued hardest
Rejects splitting the team on the basis of how long projects behave in this organisation
execution: Designs a checkpoint with a defined stop condition rather than asking for trust
Surfaces the 40% overrun risk in advance
Uses the verification strategy as the answer to the previous failure
communication: Gives the CRO something dated to sell rather than asking him to absorb silence
Addresses the committee's memory of the last rewrite directly instead of hoping it does not come up

product_sense: Treats the rewrite as a purely technical decision with no commercial framing
analytics: Ignores the pipeline attribution or the hardware cost when comparing options
prioritization: Splits the team to avoid a hard conversation
Defers indefinitely without acknowledging the problem grows with customer data size
execution: Asks for two quarters of trust with no checkpoint or stop condition
Omits the engineer's stated overrun risk from the recommendation
Proposes shipping scenario comparison on the old engine despite being told it would be unusable
communication: Does not engage with the CRO's constraint at all
Does not acknowledge the previous failed rewrite that several committee members lived through

learnTakeaway.title: Make long work falsifiable
learnTakeaway.body: The objection to a two-quarter rewrite is rarely really about two quarters — it is that nobody can tell whether it is going well until it is over, and organisations that have been burned once will not buy that again. The most valuable thing you can add to a long technical project is not scope reduction but an early, cheap, measurable signal of whether the approach works, plus a pre-agreed condition under which you stop. That turns a request for trust into a sequence of decisions, which is a much easier thing for a committee to approve.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: Full rewrite with four engineers, and I'd structure the ask around the real objection. The CRO's problem isn't two quarters, it's two quarters he can't see into — and this committee watched a rewrite run fourteen months and get abandoned. The difference is the parallel run: from about week six we can diff output against production data and measure recompute on a real 400k-SKU dataset. So: a week-8 checkpoint with agreed thresholds, and if we miss them we stop and take the narrow rewrite. Hardware is $1.08m a year for 30% and that road ends. I'd present this as two to two-and-a-half quarters.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: I'd take the one-quarter narrow rewrite, and it's the worse technical answer chosen for organisational reasons. The engineering case for the full rewrite is sound, but this committee abandoned a rewrite three years ago and two half-migrated modules are still in the codebase, so the budget for 'trust us for two quarters' is near zero and the CRO is 11% behind. A quarter that halves slow-plan tickets and unblocks the $2.1m item is something I can get approved this week. It raises the later data-model cost to about two and a half quarters, and I'd say that rather than let it look free.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: The engineering case is strong but the CRO is right that we cannot go dark for two quarters when we are behind on growth. I would put two engineers on the rewrite and keep two on roadmap items so we deliver something visible each quarter while the platform work progresses. It takes longer but everyone gets something.
